items.title: A zero that should have been an error
items.result: published video: https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:ugcPost:7515852855635951618/ (13 Oct 22:20, from the PC)
items.caption: (posted)

Four ads, each reaching about 10,000 people, do not add up to 40,000 people reached.

The real number could be 9,000. It could be 30,000. Nobody who adds the four numbers together can know.

Reach counts people, not views. Someone who saw all four ads is one person, but a sum counts them four times. The campaign might have reached 9,000 people or 30,000. Only the platform, which knows who is who, can tell you.

Spend adds up. Impressions add up. Clicks add up. Reach doesn't, across ads or across days. A week's reach isn't seven daily reaches added together either: the same people come back on Tuesday. The only honest figure is the one the platform gives for that exact set of ads and that exact date range.

It sounds small until a client puts your monthly report next to Ads Manager and the numbers don't match.

Adspenta never adds reach up. Where a total would need it, the screen shows no number rather than a wrong one.

Worth checking: where does the "total reach" in your client reports come from?

P.S. Same trap with frequency: an average frequency across ads isn't the campaign's frequency either, because it's reach underneath. If a tool shows one, ask how it was calculated.

My backups stopped twice. Nothing failed either time. That was the problem.

The second time, the setting that tells the nightly job where to send the off-site copy had gone missing from the server. So the job did exactly what it was told: nothing. Then it finished "successfully".

No error, no alert, every log green. For about two days, the only backup sat on the same disk as the database. It was found by accident.

Error alerts only fire when something fails. A job that quietly stops doing its work never fails.

So I changed what counts as an alarm. In Adspenta's operator console, "no backup ever recorded" is red, not an empty row. A last good copy older than 26 hours is amber. Not 24: the job runs at 03:20, and a warning that shows up every single morning stops being seen. And if the off-site copy used to work and now can't run, the job refuses and alerts instead of quietly doing nothing.

Agencies have the same shape of problem: the tag that stopped firing, the rule that stopped running, the client report nobody noticed didn't go out.

What's the thing in your agency that would break without making a sound?

P.S. The detail that made it worse: the nightly local backups kept working the whole time, only the off-site copy stopped. One combined "backups OK" light would have stayed green. So the console now shows the two halves separately.

For months, Undo in Adspenta never worked. More than 1,300 automated tests passed every time.

Here's why. Adspenta has a cooldown: after it changes something in an ad account, it won't touch the same thing again for a while. That stops a tool from reacting to its own last change, which is how automated rules end up going in circles.

But an undo is a change too. It comes right after the change it reverses. So it always landed inside the cooldown, and the cooldown refused it. Every single time.

The tests missed it because a test for Undo set the cooldown to zero first, to keep the test simple. It was testing a setup no customer would ever run.

A review found it in mid-September. Now a reversal is exempt from the cooldown of the change it reverses.

Two lessons, really one: a safety rule can block its own way out, and a test that changes the settings to make itself easier is testing something else.

If your agency runs automated rules with a cooldown, try undoing a change right after one fires. Just to see what happens.

P.S. There was a second half to the bug: one refused undo left the change marked as "being undone" forever. Both are fixed. Since then, a green test run makes me ask one more question: what did the test switch off to pass?

items.title: 10 checks before a change touches a client's ad account
items.caption:
Before a tool changes anything in a client's ad account, it should be able to answer 10 questions.

These are the 10 checks behind every change in Adspenta. They work as a checklist with any tool, or with a person and a spreadsheet.

The two I'd start with if you only take two:
Is this account allowed to change at all? Live changes should be off for every account until someone turns them on, one account at a time.
Did the platform confirm it? "Sent" is not "done". Read the value back before calling it done.

The full list is in the document.

Which check does your current setup skip?

P.S. The one people argue with most is number 5: a cooldown picked from a list, never typed into a box. Short version: a typed "1" is how a cooldown turns into a loop. Full story next week.

"At most 4 changes a day", set by two agencies on the same ad account, is 8.

It happens: a brand moves to a new agency and the old one keeps access for a few weeks. Or prospecting goes to one agency and retargeting to another, in the same Meta account.

If both agencies used Adspenta, each would set its own limits. Say both choose "at most 4 changes a day on this account". That's 8 changes a day, and neither agency can see the other's 4, because each limit only counts its own changes.

Two sets of guardrails on one account aren't two safeguards. They're none.

I first tried to design a way for the two agencies to coordinate. Every version was fragile. So I did the boring thing: if the same Meta ad account is connected in two agencies, neither can make live changes until one of them lets go.

Boring rules are the ones that hold.

Before you set any rule on a new client's account, ask who else still has access to it.

P.S. The first version of this check was too strict: it blocked a brand-new agency because of an old, disconnected copy of the same account. Now it only counts an agency that can actually make changes right now.

A double-click on Send emailed the client twice.

Adspenta drafts the update an agency sends to its client. A person reads it, edits it, and presses Send.

A review at the end of September found that a double-click sent the email once per click. Two clicks, two identical emails in the client's inbox.

Nobody received one. No customer had used the feature yet. But it's exactly what a client notices, and it makes an agency look careless for something it didn't do.

The same review found the opposite bug right next to it: an old path that marked an email "sent" and logged it, without sending anything.

Same lie, both directions. The screen said one thing, the inbox said another.

Now the draft is claimed the moment Send is pressed, so a second click finds nothing to send. And if the sending service doesn't confirm, the screen doesn't say "Sent". It asks you to check your Sent folder.

In anything that talks to your clients, "sent" should mean they got it, once.

P.S. That review found 97 problems in all, 11 of them serious. Every one is fixed and has a test that fails if it comes back. Not glamorous, but it's most of the job.

items.title: Sent is not done: the words a tool should use about your client's money
items.caption:
"Done" is the most expensive word in ad software.

When a tool changes a client's budget, there are at least six different states between "someone had an idea" and "it worked". It's easy to show only two: pending and done.

Here are six, and each one makes a different promise. The two that matter most are the ones Adspenta draws dashed, because they're not true yet:
Not sent yet: there's still time to take it back.
Unconfirmed: sent, but the platform hasn't shown the new value.

Only after the platform is read back does it say Confirmed. And 7 and 14 days later it says whether the change helped.

The document walks through all six.

Ask your tools which of these words they use. If the answer is "Done", ask which one they mean.

P.S. There's a seventh word for test mode: Simulated. A simulated change is never shown as Confirmed, anywhere. It sounds obvious. It took real work to make it true on every screen.

I deleted some test agencies and it cut off my own Meta connection.

In September I cleaned up a few test agencies in Adspenta. That night my real ad accounts stopped reading.

The error said the user had not authorised the application. The token still had 51 days left.

What happened: when you remove an agency, Adspenta hands its Meta access back, as it should. But Meta's "revoke" doesn't remove one token. It removes the whole app from that person's Facebook account. My test agencies used my Facebook login. So did my real one. Revoking one revoked them all.

The name of the call promised something small. What it did was big.

Now, before Adspenta hands access back, it checks whether the same login is still used by another active connection. If it is, it skips the call and writes down why.

For agencies it's bigger than my bug. One person's Facebook login is often holding up access to many client accounts. If that person leaves, or someone cleans up the wrong thing, everything behind it goes too. How many of your client accounts hang off one person's login?

P.S. The trade-off, stated plainly: in that case Meta keeps honouring a token we have deleted on our side. That's a smaller harm than switching off someone else's working connection, so I chose it and recorded it.

In September I set the cooldown on an ad account to zero. On the wrong account.

I had three accounts whose names differed by one space and one capital letter. The one I changed was not the one I meant.

Two things changed in Adspenta after that.

First, you can give any ad account your own name. The platform's name still shows underneath, so nobody loses track of which is which.

Second, the cooldown is no longer a box you type into. It's a list of set choices. A "1" typed into a box can be a minute when you meant an hour, and a one-minute cooldown on an automated rule is a loop: change, react to the change, change back, react again.

Free text feels flexible. In settings that move a client's money, it's mostly room for mistakes.

Has anyone in your agency ever changed the right setting on the wrong account?

P.S. The renaming is logged too: who renamed which account, and when. If a name causes a mistake later, you can see where it came from.

For months, Adspenta's creative fatigue alert said the same thing on every account: nothing found. It could never have fired.

Ad fatigue is simple to describe. The same people see the same ad too many times, they stop looking, the clicks drop, the budget keeps paying. So the alert compared how often people had seen an ad against a limit, and raised a flag when the number went over.

Except it compared a 7-day frequency with a limit written for a single day. Seven days of views against a one-day ceiling. The number was always far under the line. On every account, every morning, the alert checked, found nothing, and said so. Calmly.

Nobody celebrates a quiet alarm, but nobody questions it either. "No fatigue found" reads like good news.

It was found in a review, not by a complaint. The fix was one line: compare like with like. The day it went in, the alert fired on two ads that had been tired for weeks.

The lesson I keep: when an alert has never fired, that's not evidence it works. Check its units before you trust its silence.

If your agency runs its own rules or scripts, which one has never fired? Start there.

items.title: Did the change work? The life of one change, from idea to measured
items.caption:
Most ad tools suggest a change and never ask whether it worked.

This document follows one change in Adspenta from the first read to the last check: found on the daily read, proposed with the numbers, approved by a person, sent, read back from the platform, and then measured again 7 and 14 days later against that account's own baseline.

The last step is the one almost nobody does. It gives one of four honest answers: improved, worse, no change, or not enough data yet. "Not enough data" is an answer, not a failure. Pretending to know is the failure.

None of this needs Adspenta. A spreadsheet with a date, a before number and two after numbers does the same job for any agency.

When was the last time you went back to a change you made a month ago and checked?

Adspenta's AI can read every connected ad account. It has zero ways to change one.

That was a decision, not a limitation. When I added a chat to the product, the obvious version was an assistant that does things: "pause this ad", "lower that budget". Agencies I spoke to in September were clear that this was exactly what they did not want near a client's money.

So the chat can look things up, explain a number, and write a proposal for a person to approve. The part that actually sends a change to Meta or Google is separate, and the AI has no path to it. That separation is checked automatically every time the software is built, so it cannot drift back quietly.

It makes the product less impressive in a demo. It makes it something an agency can put in front of a client and explain in one sentence: the AI talks, the software does, and a person says yes in between.

What would you let an AI do in a client's ad account without asking you first?

The guide I was about to send my first outside user was 424 lines long. Nobody reads 424 lines.

It was written the day before the first agency got their password, in September. It explained everything: every screen, every setting, every word in the interface. It was complete, and it was useless, because the person reading it had a client call in an hour.

I cut it to 216 lines by asking one question of every paragraph: does this stop a mistake? If not, it went.

What stayed: the difference between live and simulated mode. What the status words mean, so "Unconfirmed" doesn't get read as "done". The budget ceiling that bites first, so the first refusal isn't a surprise.

What went: the tour. Where the buttons are, what the colours mean, how proud I am of the ledger.

Client onboarding docs work the same way. A new client doesn't need a tour of your agency. They need the three mistakes that would make the first month go wrong, and how to avoid them.

How long is the document you send a new client, and when did you last cut it?

In September I almost built a page on adspenta.com that only AI chatbots would see.

The idea was tempting. More people ask ChatGPT and the others "which tool does X" every month. A page written for the bots, full of the exact phrases they look for, hidden from humans who'd find it odd. It would have taken an afternoon.

I didn't build it. Showing bots different content from what people see is cloaking. Search engines have punished it for twenty years, and the AI assistants lean on those same search indexes. The shortcut would have put at risk the one channel it was meant to win.

What I did instead is boring: one plain page that says what Adspenta is, who it's for, and what it refuses to do, readable by a person and a bot alike, plus a small text file that tells the bots where to look.

If an agency pitches you "AI search optimisation" and the plan involves content your customers never see, that's the same trick with a new name.

Has anyone pitched your agency something like this yet?

On 9 September 2026 Google stopped issuing developer tokens for the Google Ads API. For a small tool like mine, that changed who holds the keys.

For years, any software that read or changed Google Ads accounts needed a developer token tied to a manager account. Google reviewed it, gave it an access level, and that token sat in the code.

Since September, access follows the Google Cloud project instead. Existing levels were moved over automatically. The token header still works, but Google says it's ignored and will go. New applications go through the Cloud Console, pending ones were closed and had to be resubmitted, and new access now comes with brand verification.

For Adspenta it meant a few days of checking that the access landed on the right project and that the right people own it. Not dramatic. Easy to miss.

For an agency choosing a tool, it changes one question. It used to be "does this tool have Google Ads API access?" Now it's "whose Cloud project does this tool run on, and who controls it?" If the answer is one freelancer's personal account, so is your access to your clients' data.

Worth asking your tools this week, before it matters.
